title: Chronicum
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0162.stoa005.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: diuque, nempe usque ad Cadmi ætatem, nullis prorsus litte- ris usi suut : primus enim dicitur Cadmus litterarum elementa e Phoenicum regione cis attulisse. Sane et in Platonis libro jure castigat Ægyptius ille Solonem : < 0 Solon ***, inquit, Græci semper pueri estis, neque senex Græcus unquam invenitur . ideoque priscorum temporum doctrinam ncino a vobis discere queat (5)... » Porro et Ægyptioruxi multæ feruntur insanæ historiae, itemque Chaldæorum.
passages.english: and for a long time, indeed down to the age of Cadmus, they used no letters at all; for Cadmus is said to have been the first to bring the elements of letters over here from the region of the Phoenicians. Indeed, in a book of Plato that Egyptian rightly rebukes Solon: "O Solon," he says, "you Greeks are always children, and an old Greek is never found; and therefore no one could learn the learning of ancient times from you..." Moreover, many senseless histories of the Egyptians are reported, and likewise of the Chaldaeans.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'suut' read as 'sunt', 'ncino' as 'nemo', 'Ægyptioruxi' as 'Ægyptiorum'. The asterisks after 'Solon' and the numeral '(5)' are edition marks and are omitted.

passages.original: t. Sibylla ait, omnes homines una lingua utenles (3) turrim celsissimam exstruxisse, ut in cœlum conscenderent : Deum vero fortissimum vento afflato eamdem turrim dejecisse, peculiaremque singulis sermonem tribuisse, ideoque et urbem Babylonem esse appellatam.
passages.english: The Sibyl says that all men, using one language, built a very lofty tower in order to climb up into heaven; but God, most mighty, blowing a wind upon it, threw down that same tower and gave each [people] its own particular speech, and that for this reason the city was also called Babylon.
passages.notes: The opening "t." is apparently a stray mark and has been omitted. "utenles" read as "utentes".

passages.original: Quarta dynastia Memphitarum regum XVII ex alia regia familia, quorum tertius Supbis, maximæ pyramidis auctor; qUam quidem Herodotus (5) a Chcopc structam ait qui in deos ipsos superbie.. bat: tum facti poenitens sacrum librum conscribc- Lat, quem Ægyptii instar magni thesauri habere se putabant. De reliquis regibus nihil memorabile litteris mandatum est.
passages.english: The fourth dynasty: seventeen kings of Memphis from another royal family. The third of them was Suphis, the builder of the greatest pyramid; Herodotus indeed says it was built by Cheops. He was arrogant even toward the gods themselves; then, repenting of this, he wrote a sacred book, which the Egyptians considered they possessed as a great treasure. Of the remaining kings nothing memorable has been committed to writing.
passages.notes: Text has Supbis/Chcopc; read Suphis/Cheope. "superbie.. bat" read as "superbiebat", and "conscribc- Lat" as "conscripsit" or "conscribebat".

passages.original: Agc # vero initium capiam ab Ægyptiorum litteris, quas quidem ipsas per se in mediuin afferrc non licet : verum ManeLho genere Ægyptius, vir Græca eruditionc imbutus, uti vel inde appard quod patriam historiam Graeca lingua conscripsit, e templorum, ut ipse ait, interpretatus monumentis, quique etiam Herodotum sæpe arguit in Ægyptiacis rebus ob inscitiam mentitum ; hie I inquam, Manctho primo (9) Ægyptiacarum rerum ita de nobis. scribit. Utar autcin ejus verbis, quippe qui ipsummet testem. produco. Regem, inquit, habuimus (10) Timaeum (1) nomine.
passages.english: Now let me begin from the writings of the Egyptians, which it is not possible to bring forward directly in themselves. But Manetho, an Egyptian by birth, a man steeped in Greek learning, as is evident even from the fact that he wrote his country's history in the Greek language, translating it, as he himself says, from the records of the temples, and who also often convicts Herodotus of having told falsehoods in Egyptian matters out of ignorance: this Manetho, I say, writes thus about us in the first [book] of his Egyptian history. I shall use his own words, since I am bringing forward the witness himself. "We had," he says, "a king named Timaeus."
passages.notes: Many scanning errors corrected (e.g. ManeLho, appard, autcin). The first-person "about us" reflects that this passage is quoted from Josephus (Against Apion), who speaks for the Jews.

passages.original: Quarta dynastia Memphitarum regum XVII ex alia regia familia, quorum tertius Suphis, maximæ pyramidis auctor; qUam quidem Herodotus (o) a Cheope structam ait qui in deos ipsos superbiebat: tum facti pœnitens sacrum librum conscribc- Lat, quem Ægyptii instar magni thesauri habere se putabant. De reliquis regibus nihil memorabile litteris mandatum est.
passages.english: The fourth dynasty: seventeen kings of Memphis from another royal family. The third of them was Suphis, the builder of the greatest pyramid; Herodotus indeed says it was built by Cheops. He was arrogant even toward the gods themselves; then, repenting of this, he wrote a sacred book, which the Egyptians considered they possessed as a great treasure. Of the remaining kings nothing memorable has been committed to writing.
passages.notes: Duplicate of p05633. "conscribc- Lat" read as "conscripsit".

passages.original: Age * vero initium capiam ab Ægyptiorum lilteris, quas quidem ipsas per se in medium afferre non licet : verum Manetho genere Ægyptius, vir Grseca eruditione imbutus, uti vcl inde apparet quod patriam historiam Graeca lingua conscripsit, e templorum, ut ipse ait, interpretatus monumentis, qniquc etiam Herodotum sæpe arguit in Ægyptiacis rcbus ob inscitiam mentitum; hic, inquam, Manctho primo (9) Ægyptiacarum rerum ita de nubis. scribit. Utar autcm ejus verbis, quippe qui ipsummet testem. produco. Regem, inquit, habuimus (10) Timæum (1) nomine.
passages.english: Now let me begin from the writings of the Egyptians, which it is not possible to bring forward directly in themselves. But Manetho, an Egyptian by birth, a man steeped in Greek learning, as is evident even from the fact that he wrote his country's history in the Greek language, translating it, as he himself says, from the records of the temples, and who also often convicts Herodotus of having told falsehoods in Egyptian matters out of ignorance: this Manetho, I say, writes thus about us in the first [book] of his Egyptian history. I shall use his own words, since I am bringing forward the witness himself. "We had," he says, "a king named Timaeus."
passages.notes: Duplicate of p05634. "nubis" read as "nobis".

passages.original: Tertius Apis, de quo regio illa Apia dicta est, annis XXXV. Ea tempestate apud Ægyptios dominatum tenuit Josephus, quem Hebraei memorant.
passages.english: The third, Apis, from whom that region was called Apia, [reigned] thirty-five years. At that time Joseph, whom the Hebrews record, held power among the Egyptians.

passages.original: Hic dextrum est catalogum etiam Atheniensium regum attexere, e certioribus veterum memo* riis prælibata summatim h storia. Primus ab Atheniensibus memoratur Ogygus, in cujus ætatem ingens illud et perantiquum diluvium incurrisse fertur. Hujus aequalis habetur Phoroneus, Inachi filius, Argivorum rex, quem ipse Plato in Timæo suo (3) commemorat his verbis : « Cum eos commovere studeret (4) ad sermonem de hujus urbis antiquitatibus, vetustissima narrare aggressus est de pri- mo illo Phoroneo, de Niobe, deque rebus quæ diluvium consecutæ sunt.
passages.english: Here it is fitting also to append a list of the Athenian kings, after first touching briefly on the history from the more reliable records of the ancients. The first remembered by the Athenians is Ogygus, in whose time that great and very ancient flood is said to have occurred. Contemporary with him is held to be Phoroneus, son of Inachus, king of the Argives, whom Plato himself mentions in his Timaeus in these words: "When he wished to draw them into talk about the antiquities of this city, he set about relating the most ancient things, about that first Phoroneus, about Niobe, and about the events that followed the flood."

passages.original: Verumtamen Aristodemus Eleus (9) refert, exacta vicesilna et septima olympiade (postquam agon ab Iphito institutus fuerat) coeptos esse scribi victores, cum antea ob velerum incuriam nemo ruisset litteris consignatus : donec vigesima octava (I) olympiade cum vicisset stadium Coroebus Eleus, ipse primus in album relatus est, eamque primam olympiadem habitam esse, ex qua Graeci sua tempora supputant. Arislodemo suffragatur et .Polybius. At Callimachus ait, XIII (2) olympiades post Iphitum non esse 3cripto commendatas, nempe usque ad quartam decimam quam vicit Corœbus. Multi vero affirmant, inter agonem, quem Hercules Alcmena instituerit, primamque scriptam olympiadem interjectos esse annos CCCCLIX.
passages.english: Nevertheless Aristodemus of Elis reports that it was after the twenty-seventh Olympiad had passed (counting from when the contest was instituted by Iphitus) that the victors began to be recorded, since before that, through the carelessness of the ancients, no one had been entered in writing; until in the twenty-eighth Olympiad, when Coroebus of Elis won the stadium race, he was the first entered in the register, and that was reckoned the first Olympiad, from which the Greeks compute their dates. Polybius too agrees with Aristodemus. But Callimachus says that thirteen Olympiads after Iphitus were not committed to writing, that is, up to the fourteenth, which Coroebus won. Many, however, affirm that between the contest which Heracles son of Alcmena instituted and the first recorded Olympiad, 459 years intervened.
passages.notes: The numeral XIII after Callimachus is marked with a footnote and may be corrupt; it conflicts with "fourteenth".

passages.original: 2. Sed enim philosophus Aristoteles ait, Achaeos aliquot Troja revertentes, dum Maleum (16) navigarent, sæva hieme correptos, ventis bac illac per universum maris tractum vagari coactos, tandem locum Opicae tenuisse nomine Latium, quod Tyrrheni maris vastitati adjacet.
passages.english: 2. But the philosopher Aristotle says that some Achaeans returning from Troy, while sailing around Malea, were caught by a fierce storm and, forced by the winds to wander this way and that over the whole expanse of the sea, at last reached a place in Opica named Latium, which lies beside the vast Tyrrhenian Sea.
passages.notes: Opica: the land of the Opici (Osci) in Italy.

passages.original: at Quintus Fabius in annum octavae olympiadis primum ; denique Calo Porcius (qui etsi Graecorum temporum regulam non sequitur, curiosus tamen, quam qui maxime, in antiqua historia colligenda est) annis CDXXXII Iliaco bello recentiorem affirmat : quod tempus si ad Eratosthenis chronologiam exigatur , in primum anuum olympiadis septimæ incurret. Jam quod sanis regulis utatur Eratosthenes, et quomodo liceat Pomana tempora ad Graecorum rationes supputare, alio docui tractatu (i).
passages.english: but Quintus Fabius [places it] in the first year of the eighth Olympiad; finally Cato Porcius (who, although he does not follow the Greek rule of dating, is nevertheless as careful as anyone in collecting ancient history) asserts [that it is] 432 years later than the Trojan War: if this period is measured against the chronology of Eratosthenes, it will fall in the first year of the seventh Olympiad. Now, that Eratosthenes uses sound rules, and how one may reckon Roman dates by the Greek systems, I have shown in another treatise.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'Calo' read as 'Cato', 'anuum' as 'annum', 'Pomana' as 'Romana'. The '(i)' is a footnote mark and is omitted. The subject is the founding of Rome, as the preceding context shows. The first-person 'I have shown in another treatise' matches Dionysius of Halicarnassus (named in the following context), whom this passage appears to quote.

passages.original: Denique quid Psalterio canorius, quod in morem nostri Flacci, et Graeci Pindari, nunc iambo currit, nunc Alcaico personat, nunc Sapphico tumet, nunc semipede ingreditur? Quid Deuteronomii et Isaiæ cantico pulchrius? Quid Salomone gravius? Quid perfectius Job? Quae omnia hexametris et pentametris versibus, ut Josephus et Origenes scribunt, apud suos composita decurrunt. Hæc cum Graece legimus, aliud quiddam sonant, cum Latine, penitus non cohaerent. Quod si cui non videtur linguae gratiam interpretatione mutari, Homerun. ad verbum exprimat in Latinum.
passages.english: Finally, what is more melodious than the Psalter, which, in the manner of our Flaccus and the Greek Pindar, now runs in iambs, now rings in Alcaics, now swells in Sapphics, now advances with a half-foot? What is more beautiful than the songs of Deuteronomy and Isaiah? What is weightier than Solomon? What more perfect than Job? All of these, as Josephus and Origen write, run in hexameter and pentameter verses composed in their own language. When we read these in Greek they sound somewhat different; when in Latin, they do not hang together at all. But if anyone thinks that the grace of a language is not altered by translation, let him render Homer word for word into Latin.
passages.notes: Flaccus: Horace.

passages.original: Si autem Cecropis, consequenter et Moysi, qui cum Cecrope fuit. Post hunc enim scribiLur diluviuln sub Deucalione, incendiutn sub Phaethonte, Erichthonius Vulcani et Terræ Clius, Dardanusque qui Dardaniam condidit, de quo Homerus : Quem primum genuit coelesti Jupiter arce.
passages.english: But if [it is the age] of Cecrops, then consequently [it is] also [the age] of Moses, who lived at the same time as Cecrops. For after him are recorded the flood under Deucalion, the conflagration under Phaethon, Erichthonius the son of Vulcan and Earth, and Dardanus who founded Dardania, of whom Homer [says]: "Whom Jupiter first begot from his heavenly citadel."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: scribiLur = scribitur, diluviuln = diluvium, incendiutn = incendium, Clius = filius. The quoted Homeric line (cf. Iliad 20.215) is given here in a Latin version.

passages.original: Phoroneus Inachi filius et Niobae, primus leges judiciaque constituit. Quidam hujus filiam Niobem arbitrantur. Horum temporum quasi vafde antiquorum Plato in Timæo meminit ita dicens : < Et aliquando volens eos provocare in sermones de temporibus antiquis, quae unicuique civitati apud veteres accidissent, de Phoroneo, qui primus hoc nomine appellatus et, de Niobe, et his qui post diluvium fuerunt.
passages.english: Phoroneus, son of Inachus and Niobe, was the first to establish laws and courts. Some think Niobe was his daughter. Plato in the Timaeus mentions these times as very ancient, saying: "And once, wishing to draw them into talk about ancient times, [about] what had befallen each city among the ancients, [he spoke] of Phoroneus, who was the first to be called by this name, and of Niobe, and of those who lived after the flood.
passages.notes: vafde read as valde. The quotation is unfinished at the end of the passage; its closing mark follows in the context.

passages.original: k Diluvium quod sub Deucalione in Thessalia, et incendium quod sub Pbaethonte in i£ thiopia factuln est, et aliae multæ pestilentias locales, ut Plato memorat, fuerunt.
passages.english: The flood that took place under Deucalion in Thessaly, and the conflagration that took place under Phaethon in Ethiopia, and many other local disasters, as Plato records, occurred [at this time].
passages.notes: Leading 'k' taken as a footnote mark. Scanning errors: Pbaethonte = Phaethonte, i£ thiopia = Aethiopia, factuln = factum.

passages.original: i Tyrus condita ante templum Hierosolymorum annis CCXLI, ut scribit Josephus in quarto.
passages.english: Tyre was founded 241 years before the temple of Jerusalem, as Josephus writes in [his] fourth [book].
passages.notes: Leading 'i' taken as a footnote mark.

passages.original: Dicitur autem Antaeus terræ filius, quia solus palaestricae artis certaminum, quae in terra exercentur, scientissimus erat; et ob id videbatur a terra matre adjuvari. Hydram autem calidissimam fuisse sophistriam asserit Plato.
passages.english: Antaeus is called the son of Earth because he alone was most skilled in the contests of the wrestling art, which are practised on the ground; and for that reason he seemed to be helped by his mother Earth. Plato asserts that the Hydra was a most cunning sophistry.
passages.notes: 'calidissimam' (literally 'hottest') is taken in its sense 'most crafty', i.e. callidissimam.

passages.original: Secundum Sicyonios, a vicesimo secundo anno Europis, similiter anni DCCCXXXV. A nativitate vero Moysir, anni CCCCX. A primo anno Cecropis, qui primus apud Atticam regnavit, usque ad captivitatem Trojæ. et usque ad vicesimum tertium annum Menesthei, cujus Homerus meminit, anni CCCLXXV. Similiter a XXXV anso ætatis Moysi, fiunt anni CCCLXXV.
passages.english: According to the Sicyonians, from the twenty-second year of Europs, likewise 835 years. From the birth of Moses, 410 years. From the first year of Cecrops, who was the first to reign in Attica, up to the capture of Troy, and up to the twenty-third year of Menestheus, whom Homer mentions, 375 years. Likewise from the thirty-fifth year of Moses' age come 375 years.
passages.notes: Moysir read as Moysi, anso as anno. The figure of 410 years from Moses' birth sits oddly with the later reckoning from his 35th year; the numbers may be corrupt.

passages.original: b Pyrrbus Delphis in tempto Apollinis ab Oreste occiditur proditione sacerdolis Macharei : quo tempore etiam quidam Homerum fuisse dicunt.
passages.english: Pyrrhus is killed by Orestes at Delphi in the temple of Apollo through the treachery of the priest Machareus; some also say Homer lived at this time.
passages.notes: Leading 'b' taken as a footnote mark. Scanning errors: Pyrrbus = Pyrrhus, tempto = templo, sacerdolis = sacerdotis.

passages.original: Carthago secundum nonnullos condita a Didone. Alii suprascriptum tempus vindicant: quod Virgilius non esse verum ostendit, qui Didonem se interfecisse ait.
passages.english: Carthage was founded by Dido, according to some. Others claim the time written above; Virgil shows this is not true, since he says that Dido killed herself.
passages.notes: The reasoning is compressed. Presumably Virgil's account, in which Dido kills herself for Aeneas, makes her a contemporary of Aeneas, against the later date. That would mean Virgil supports the earlier date, which is not what the sentence plainly says. The sense is uncertain.

passages.original: a Ionica emigratio, in qua quidam Homerum fuissc scribunt.
passages.english: The Ionian migration, at which time some write that Homer lived.
passages.notes: Leading 'a' taken as a footnote mark. fuissc = fuisse.

passages.original: II Hesiodus insignis babetur, ut vult Porphyrius.
passages.english: Hesiod is regarded as famous [at this time], as Porphyry holds.
passages.notes: Leading 'II' is likely a marginal mark. babetur = habetur.

passages.original: I Cyri Persae ascensus, de quo scribit Xenophon.
passages.english: The expedition up-country of Cyrus the Persian, about which Xenophon writes.
passages.notes: Initial 'I' is probably a stray marginal letter or footnote mark and has been omitted. 'Ascensus' renders the Greek 'anabasis'.

passages.original: I Theophrastus philosophus agnoscitur, qui divinitate loquendi, ut ait Cicero, nomen accepit.
passages.english: Theophrastus the philosopher becomes known, who, as Cicero says, received his name from the divine quality of his speech.
passages.notes: Initial 'I' omitted as a stray mark.

passages.original: i Menander primam fabulam cogno nento 'Οργήν docens superat.
passages.english: Menander, producing his first play, entitled *Orgē* [Anger], wins the prize.
passages.notes: Initial 'i' omitted as a stray mark. 'cogno nento' read as 'cognomento'.

passages.original: Plotiue Gallus primus Romae Latinam rhetoricam docuit : de quo Cicero sic refert : < Mcmona tenoo pueris nohis primum Latine docere coepisse Plolium quemdam. »
passages.english: Plotius Gallus was the first to teach Latin rhetoric at Rome. About him Cicero reports as follows: "I remember that when we were boys a certain Plotius first began to teach in Latin."
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected: 'Plotiue' read as 'Plotius', 'Mcmona tenoo pueris nohis' as 'Memoria teneo pueris nobis', 'Plolium' as 'Plotium'.

passages.original: Ea, quae de Catilina, Ccthego, Lentulo, et consule Cicerone Sallustius scribit, et Livius, boc gesta sunt tcmpore.
passages.english: The events that Sallust and Livy write about concerning Catiline, Cethegus, Lentulus, and Cicero as consul took place at this time.
passages.notes: 'Ccthego', 'boc' and 'tcmpore' read as 'Cethego', 'hoc' and 'tempore'.

passages.original: Caius Cornelius Gallus, de quo Virgilius scribit in Bucolicis.
passages.english: Gaius Cornelius Gallus, about whom Virgil writes in the Bucolics.

passages.original: d Pilato de Christianorum dogmate ad Tiberium referente, Tiberius retulit ad senatum, ut inter cætera sacra reciperetur. Verum cum ex consulto patrum Christianos eliminari Urbe placuisset, Tiberius per edictum accusatoribus Christianorum comminatus est mortem. Scribit Tertullianus in Apologetico.
passages.english: When Pilate reported to Tiberius about the teaching of the Christians, Tiberius referred [the matter] to the senate, so that it might be received among the other cults. But when, by decree of the fathers, it had been resolved that the Christians be expelled from the City, Tiberius threatened the accusers of the Christians with death by an edict. Tertullian writes [this] in the Apologeticum.
passages.notes: Initial 'd' omitted as a stray mark.

passages.original: k Toto orbe Romano, sicuti Pbilo scribit, et Josephus, in synagogis Judaeorum statuae et imagines et arae Caii Caesaris consecratae.
passages.english: Throughout the whole Roman world, as Philo and Josephus write, statues, images and altars of Gaius Caesar were consecrated in the synagogues of the Jews.
passages.notes: Initial 'k' omitted as a stray mark.

passages.original: d Sub Felice procuratore Judææ multi exatiterunt, qui populum sua persuasione deciperent : in queis et Ægyptius quidam pseudoprophetes fuit : qui plurimos sibi associans, in ipso magnarum rerum conata per exercitum Felicis opprimitur. Scribit Josephus consentanea apostolorum Actibus, in quibus Pam. dicitur a tribuno : Nonne tu es Ægyptius, qui ante hes diss concitasti et eduxisti in desertum quatuor millia virorum t
passages.english: Under Felix, procurator of Judaea, many arose who deceived the people by their persuasion. Among them there was also a certain Egyptian false prophet, who gathered very many to himself, and in the very attempt at great undertakings was crushed by Felix's army. Josephus writes [an account] in agreement with the Acts of the Apostles, in which the tribune says to Paul: "Are you not the Egyptian who some days ago stirred up and led out into the desert four thousand men?"
passages.notes: Initial 'd' omitted. 'exatiterunt' read as 'exstiterunt', 'conata' as 'conatu', 'Pam.' as 'Paulo', 'hes diss' as 'hos dies'; the final 't' is taken as a stray mark for a question mark.

passages.original: i Titus, Judaea capta et Hierosolymis subversis, DC millia virorum interficit. Josephus vero scribit undecies centena millia fame et gladio periisse, et alia centum miliia captivorum publice venundata. Ut autem tanta multitudo Hierosolymis reperiretur, causam azymorum fuisse refert : ob quae ex omni gente Judaei ad templum confluentes, urbe quasi carcere sunt reclusi.
passages.english: Titus, after capturing Judaea and overthrowing Jerusalem, kills six hundred thousand men. Josephus, however, writes that eleven hundred thousand perished by famine and sword, and that another hundred thousand captives were publicly sold. He reports that the reason so great a multitude was found in Jerusalem was [the feast of] Unleavened Bread: because of it the Jews had flocked to the temple from every nation and were shut up in the city as if in a prison.
passages.notes: Initial 'i' omitted as a stray mark.

passages.original: k Joannem apostolum, usque ad Trajani tempora Irenaeus episcopus permansisse scribit : R. DCCCL. post quem auditores ejus insignes fuerunt Papias, Hierapolitanus episcopus, et Polycarpus, Smyrnaeus, et Ignatius, Antiochenus.
passages.english: Bishop Irenaeus writes that the apostle John lived on until the times of Trajan. R. 850. After him his distinguished hearers were Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, Polycarp of Smyrna, and Ignatius of Antioch.
passages.notes: The initial 'k' appears to be a marginal or footnote letter and has been omitted. 'R. DCCCL.' is unclear; it may be a chronological marker (perhaps a year count), and is given as printed.

passages.original: d Plinius Secundus, cum quamdam provinciam regeret, et in magistratu suo plurimos Christianorum interfecisset, multitudine eorum perterritus quæsivit a Trajano quid facto opus esset, nuntians ei, præter obstinationem non sacrificandi, et antelucanos coetus ad canendum cuidam Christo ut Deo, nibil apua eos reperiri: praeterea ad confoederandam disciplinam vetari ab iis homicidia, furta, adulteria, latrocinia et his similia. Ad quae commotus Trajanus rescripsit, hoc genus quidem inquirendum non p<sc, oblatos vero puniri oportere. Tertullianus refert in Apologetico suo.
passages.english: Pliny the Younger, when he was governing a certain province and had put to death a great many Christians during his term of office, was alarmed by their number and asked Trajan what ought to be done. He reported to him that, apart from their obstinate refusal to sacrifice and their gatherings before dawn to sing to a certain Christ as to a god, nothing was found among them; moreover, to strengthen their discipline, murders, thefts, adulteries, robberies and the like were forbidden among them. Moved by this, Trajan wrote back that this class of people should not indeed be sought out, but that those brought forward ought to be punished. Tertullian reports [this] in his Apology.
passages.notes: The initial 'd' is taken as a stray marginal letter and omitted. Scanning errors corrected: 'nibil apua' read as 'nihil apud'; 'p<sc' read as 'esse'. 'Plinius Secundus' is rendered as Pliny the Younger (Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus).

passages.original: Pestilens morbus multas totius orbis provincias occupavit, maximeque Alexandriam et AEgyptum, ut scribit Dionysius, et Cypriani De mortalitate testis est tiber.
passages.english: A pestilential disease spread over many provinces of the whole world, and above all Alexandria and Egypt, as Dionysius writes; and Cyprian's book On Mortality is a witness [to it].
passages.notes: 'tiber' read as 'liber' (book).

passages.original: BUC USQUE HISTORIAM SCRIBIT EUSEBIUS PAMPHILI MARTYRIS CONTUBERNALIS, CUI NOS ISTA SUBJECIMUS.
passages.english: UP TO THIS POINT EUSEBIUS, COMPANION OF THE MARTYR PAMPHILUS, WRITES THE HISTORY; TO IT WE HAVE ADDED WHAT FOLLOWS.
passages.notes: 'BUC' read as 'HUC'. 'Eusebius Pamphili' is traditionally understood as Eusebius the associate of Pamphilus.
